posts.c: 18 years of Tiny Desk, 100 issues of NOTION and one cover celebrating the power of music discovery. For our final cover of NOTION 100, we meet the team behind @nprmusic’s much-loved performance series to explore the thinking, taste and teamwork behind a format that has brought artists closer to their audiences. From championing emerging talent to reimagining performances from some of the world’s biggest names, Tiny Desk has spent almost two decades proving that sometimes all you need is a room, a desk and the music itself. Spotlighting emerging talent before wider recognition, and finding new ways to experience established names, Tiny Desk has consistently celebrated the people shaping music culture, often before the rest of the world catches on. In conversation with the people who make the magic happen and featuring quotes from artists who have appeared across both our worlds, we explore why authenticity matters, how the unexpected can change the way we listen, and what it means to gi

posts.c: Racked with shame as it contemplated the fact that it remained unscathed nearly a week after Halloween, a local pumpkin confirmed Friday that it was struggling with survivor’s guilt. “Of all the pumpkins that were murdered and mutilated, why was I the only one spared?” said the pumpkin, lamenting the cruel randomness that had left it unharmed while far worthier pumpkins suffered slow, horrible deaths. “They’re all gone, and I’m still here, and there’s no reason for any of it, no reason that serrated knife couldn’t have been cutting through my rind too. But here I am, and I just don’t know what to do with myself. Maybe I don’t deserve to do anything. The time for doing something was before, when the killers were taping down the carving stencils, when maybe I could’ve helped my friends. But I can’t now. There’s nothing left but this miserable unearned life that will do nothing but torture me for as long as it lasts.” At press time, the pumpkin had reportedly felt some of its burden lifte
posts.hd: Uncarved pumpkin struggling with survivor's guilt

posts.c: Matt Linehan, 43, started growing potatoes 20 years ago as one of many market-garden vegetables before deciding they were his one true farming love. He uses the f-bomb liberally to emphasize things good and bad. The word LIBERTY is tattooed on his forearm, a souvenir from his youth in the Boston punk scene. Linehan jokes that this might give people the wrong idea about his politics: “This county voted for Trump three times,” he said, “but I like living with some diversity of opinion.” On a late-October day, in the middle of the harvest, his brass eagle belt buckle was as dirt encrusted as his freshly unearthed tubers. This season contrasted sharply with recent back-to-back summers of extreme flooding. In the floods of 2023, Linehan lost 20 percent of his crop; in 2024, he lost more than 30 percent, and the floodwaters left 10-foot mud lines on the trees in some of his fields. All told, the Connecticut River washed away some $250,000 of his income over two years. Linehan farmed in Massa

The annual Taurid meteor shower is peaking, with the Southern Taurids reaching their peak on the night of November 4 and the Northern Taurids following on November 11. Although the shower may produce only a handful of shooting stars each hour, some can become brilliant fireballs bright enough to outshine Venus. With the moon providing little light during the peaks, skywatchers in both hemispheres have a good chance of catching the display. Find out how to get the best view at the link in bio. posts.c: Building connection, joy, and resilience across Vermont Over the past year, The Pride Center of Vermont board has been quietly and diligently doing the necessary work behind the scenes restructuring, re-centering and stabilizing essential programs. This week we are sharing the next chapter ahead and announcing the end to the pause of our operations with the launch of our 2026-2030 Strategic Plan. posts.c: When choosing the images for my book Reverence, I let go of the photojournalist mindset honed over decades of working as a National Geographic photographer and looked instead for the images that sparked some kind of emotion within. The Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) are truly a place of extremes, battered by powerful, nutrient-dense currents that pummel the cliffs and feed the towering kelp forests below the surface. The density of life here is staggering, especially on Steeple Jason where conservationists had the foresight to reclaim the island from sheep farming as far back as the 70s. Today the island is under the guardianship of the Wildlife Conservation Society and its natural legacy is preserved as one of the last wild places on Earth.

posts.c: Can you guess the real deal 🥒👀 As it ripens, the squirting cucumber (Ecballium elaterium) builds pressure in its fruits, allowing it to disperse its seeds as far away as possible when touched. It can launch seeds at almost 30mph and send them flying over 12 metres away! This has led to it being classified as an invasive species in many countries. Despite it being a cousin to many kitchen favourites like cucumber, watermelon and pumpkin, the squirting cucumber is inedible due to the toxic chemicals it contains. Can you guess the right audio? posts.c: Jolene Kao bought Charlotte’s iconic Old Brick Store in 2023, determined to revive the historic building as a bustling local hub, where people could shop, eat, and connect with friends and strangers alike. She installed an espresso bar, freshened up the menu of prepared food and began stocking the shelves with specialty goods in addition to classic kitchen staples. Kao also brought back something the store lacked in recent years: seating, with a long farmhouse table and stools along a coffee counter. The changes paid off. The store now hums throughout the day as workers drop by for breakfast or lunch, families pop in for milk or eggs, and visitors linger over coffee. But not everyone is celebrating the newfound energy. ✍️ Colin Flanders 📸 @hanks.pix

posts.c: 🚨 BREAKING: Introducing X-70 Fractal, @nasa’s newest experimental aircraft! This crewed, modular aircraft will allow the agency to rapidly swap out internal & external payloads to help keep pushing the frontiers of aviation technology! X-70 Fractal is a high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight. “We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.” - @nasaadmin The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions. Details: nasa.gov/aero Image caption: Gener

posts.c: It’s about time we talked about this… This tall clock was made by Thomas Wagstaffe, a renowned Quaker clockmaker based in London. It’s also one of the oldest objects in the collection at @hamptonnps, originally commissioned in 1760 by Captain Charles Ridgely. That means it’s been keeping track of time for more than 260 years, give or take. You might say it’s been around the clock a few times. Clocks like this are often called grandfather clocks, and this one is an eight-day clock, meaning it can keep ticking for eight days on a single winding. That’s a full week of punctuality, plus a day of grace. Even clocks appreciate a long weekend. Not bad for something made before electricity or smartphones. Of course, there’s a catch. The clock still needs to be wound regularly, or it will eventually run out of time. Video shows a curator wearing gloves as they carefully wind the historic clock. The sound of the winding mechanism and the clock’s chimes can be heard. NPS.
posts.hd: 1760 tall clock by Thomas Wagstaffe at Hampton

posts.c: What is Stick Season? Aside from being the title of a popular song by Vermont singer-songwriter Noah Kahan, this "mini season" has a reputation for being a gloomy time of year. It's the period of time after fall foliage has fallen and before winter snow arrives, and is often overlooked for its lack of bright leaves or classic winter beauty. But what some folks don't know is that some of the best hiking happens during Stick Season! Swipe to learn more about why we love stick season, where to hike, and what to keep in mind on trail this time of year. Visit the link in bio to explore more recommended Stick Season hikes 🔗

posts.c: If you recognize this funky little seed in the first place, you may be wondering why you haven't seen too many of them this fall... Well, we have answers! The results of our annual survey of tree nuts (called "hard mast" by foresters) looking at the crop of beech nuts, pictured here, and acorns state-wide are in: 2026 was a spotty year. Except for a few isolated sites high in the mountains and far to the north, most beech stands in Vermont saw total crop failure. Acorn production was more variable, with some sites yielding bumper crops and others just a stone's throw away yielding very little. Generally speaking, northern Vermont had a rough acorn year while southern and central Vermont faired better. It should be noted that none of this is cause for alarm! Mast production naturally cycles year to year and species to species. Wildlife like deer, turkey, bears and squirrels that depend on beech nuts and acorns in this part of their range have adapted accordingly. What this does mean is

posts.c: New Mexico elected @debhaalandnm as governor in the 2026 midterm elections, making her the first female Native American governor-elect in U.S. history. It’s a milestone in a career marked by historic firsts. From 2021 to 2025, Haaland served as the first Indigenous U.S. Secretary of the Interior, overseeing the nation’s public lands and national parks. As a member of the Pueblo of Laguna tribe, she brought a particular focus to protecting Indigenous lands and honoring their cultural significance. In 2023, Haaland was featured in our annual @womenwhotravel Power List, where she reminded travelers that to understand a destination means understanding its history: “If you are visiting another state, another county, another city, research that place. What tribes lived there prior to colonization? What tribes still live there?” You can read the full interview and find the 2023 Women Who Travel Power List at the link in bio.

posts.c: Peak cycle! A flashback from my cycle test 5 days after return to Earth from the @iss. A mask collects the air we exhale to measure the amount of CO2 we exhale (our metabolic rate), and electrodes measure our heart rate and rhythm. Our scientists and doctors use these data to ensure all is well with our cardiovascular snd respiratory systems. Just 5 days after landing and I exceeded my performance from my last test before the flight! Yet another indication that our exercise equipment on the ISS not only maintains, but can increase our fitness level even while in microgravity.

After settling into a sophisticated cabin on the Art Deco-era train, passengers are ushered into one of the opulent dining cars—complete with velvet seats and glossy marquetry—for four-course dinners prepared with seasonal ingredients. The highlight, however, are the festive evenings in the train’s bar car, named 3674. Small plants need love too! So I try to find a fun way to style them instead of just placing them in a standard terra cotta pot. Here, I took this 4” birkin philodendron and cut the perfect piece of cork to surround its roots. Instead of glue a stainless steel mesh base to the cork, like I typically do, I used a low planter to work as the base of the “pot” to hold in the soil. Obviously it has drainage holes for those that were about to ask 😉 I then dressed up the topsoil with live moss and called it a day. posts.c: If you have a room you don’t like, try making small changes over time! 🎀✨🩵 When we first redid our kitchen in 2021, I’d added some color, but mostly went with the “a white kitchen is timeless” advice. Turns out, I like living with more color! So over time I slowly added it, mostly in the form of paint. It was one small tweak at a time. No huge renovation. And I loved being able to slowly bring the space together! So if you have a room that bugs you? Change one thing. Live with it. Then change the next thing. Simple, but I promise you it works! How do you like the new yellow ceiling? 💛 Paint colors- Yellow- Sweet as Honey Pink- Beloved Pink Mint- Frosted Sage (All by Behr)

posts.c: With free agency already underway, and recognizing that Clubs will need a full offseason to operate within the cap and floor system, MLB is proposing to phase in the salary cap and floor in 2028 The projected cap and floor payrolls for 2028 would make 12 clubs increase payroll by $636M to reach the floor, and 8 clubs to decrease payroll $528M to reach the cap. Overall, this would net a $108M payroll increase Starting in 2028 would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits

posts.c: It’s leaf-peeping season. The trees have made an effort, so the least we can do is go outside and stare at them. posts.c: The ultimate group project: studying worlds beyond our own. As we get closer to the first images from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a long list of science objectives await. One way Roman will team up with Hubble is by the different ways the missions will study exoplanets. An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun. Roman will likely find hundreds of thousands exoplanets with its remarkable instruments; meanwhile, Hubble’s capabilities allow for analysis of exoplanet atmospheres. This work is part of NASA's search for life elsewhere in the universe. Plus, Roman's coronograph instrument will be able to directly image some larger exoplanets. We'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy in the weeks to come. Check the link in our bio for more on Hubble and Roman! Image description: A collage of artistic renderings of differently colored exoplanets in rows, against a black background. In the lower left, faint text reads
posts.cp: The ultimate group project: studying worlds beyond our own

posts.c: Each Tuesday this season, we're sharing stories that highlight what Rock Point means to you! "Access to the beauty and serenity that nature provides is critical for my mental health, and I have turned to Rock Point many times over the years for its ability to calm my body and recenter myself. Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, I brought my kids there for walks on a daily basis, which proved to be one of the most grounding consistent experiences that helped us find peace during extremely uncertain times. And for the past five years, my organization, Dad Guild, has accessed Rock Point on a monthly basis for its Fires with Fathers program, which provides dads and masculine-identifying caregivers with space to connect with one another on a deeper level while practicing active listening and modeling vulnerability. Rock Point is my favorite location in all of Burlington, and I cannot imagine living in this community without it." -Keegan Albaugh, Executive Director, Dad Guild Have a testimonia

posts.c: Astronauts Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) and Anil Menon of NASA will go out on their second spacewalk together on Thursday, Nov. 5, to install the eighth and final roll-out solar array to augment the International Space Station's power generation system. Here are some scenes from their previous spacewalk on Oct. 29 when they installed the seventh roll-out solar array on the orbital outpost. Pic 1) NASA astronaut Anil Menon is pictured during a spacewalk with his spacesuit's helmet lights on. posts.c: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt

posts.c: One of the densest concentrations of geysers in Yellowstone can be found in the remote Shoshone Geyser Basin, on the west side of Shoshone Lake. We visit the area in the latest Yellowstone Volcano Observatory monthly video update. 🌊 Shoshone Geyser Basin is one of the most spectacular in all of Yellowstone National Park. Located deep in the backcountry along the west side of Shoshone Lake, the area has one of the densest concentrations of geysers, second only to the Upper Geyser Basin (where Old Faithful is located). There are over 100 geysers in this region and 40 or 50 might be active at any given time. A trail takes you right by Minute Man geyser (always at the ready!), so it is quite easy to watch the frequent eruptions there. ⚡During the month of October 2026, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, which monitors and operates the Yellowstone seismic network, located 66 earthquakes. The largest was a Magnitude 2.0. Throughout 2026, there has been very little change in ground
posts.hd: Shoshone Geyser Basin in Yellowstone

posts.c: A little throwback to my broke college girl dinner era…. Honestly, I forgot how good these things are. Basically everything you want in a pizza, minus having to make an actual pizza. And yes, they’re still just as good as they were at 1AM in college. Here’s how I made them: - Split English muffins in half, drizzle with EVOO, sprinkle with garlic powder, and bake at 400°F for about 10–12 minutes, until lightly golden. - Add marinara, mozzarella, provolone, (or whatever your favorite cheese is!), dried oregano, and a little garlic salt. - Back into the oven until the cheese is melted and bubbly. - Serve with extra warm marinara for dipping. Please tell me I’m not the only one who lived on these back in the day….

posts.c: Hidden beauty 💛 Agorastos Papatsanis (@agorastospapatsanis) uses ultraviolet light to reveal the glowing yellow stems of beautiful bonnet mushrooms growing from a decaying log. On the lower slopes of Greece’s Mount Olympus, Agorastos experimented with ultraviolet (UV) illumination until it revealed the strongest fluorescent response from these mushrooms known as ‘beautiful bonnets’. While humans cannot see UV light, we can get an inkling of its effect, thanks to the phenomenon of fluorescence. Mycologists are harnessing this phenomenon to distinguish closely related species of fungi by the colours and patterns they reveal under UV. 📸 'Shedding Light' is the winner of #WPY62's Plants and Fungi category. posts.c: In this final video in our explainer series about the new deer hunting regulations this year, our Deer and Moose Project Leader Nick Fortin and Sergeant Dana Joyal from the Vermont Warden Service break down what is needed to legally take a doe in the upcoming rifle season. In order to legally take a doe during rifle season, you must have received an antlerless permit designated for a specific wildlife management unit (WMU). If you do not have a permit, you may not take a doe during the rifle season. If a hunter is unsuccessful during the rifle season, they may use that antlerless permit during the conventional muzzleloader season. Visit our website for more information about taking a doe during rifle season and all the new deer regulation changes.

posts.c: Where's the oxygen? After researchers studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies, they realized much of the oxygen they expected to see was missing. Oxygen is the main element formed by stars, and also the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium. But by using Hubble, these scientists learned that dwarf galaxies can only hang on to a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. Energy from the low-mass galaxies’ massive stars, along with galactic winds unleashed by supernova explosions, are apparently more effective at driving out the oxygen than current models predict. Read more at the link in our bio! posts.c: Día de los Muertos has its roots in an Aztec ritual known as Miccaihuitl, honoring those who have passed. The celebration coincides with the return of monarch butterflies that typically flutter away from our region and make the long flight back to Mexico to spend their winter in a warmer climate. Believed to carry the souls of the departed returning to visit their families, it’s easy to see why these beautiful, winged messengers are held sacred by so many Indigenous communities along their path. 🌼🌼🌼 El Día de los Muertos tiene sus raíces en un antiguo ritual Azteca llamado Miccaihuitl, en honor de los antepasados. Da la casualidad de que coincide con el retorno de las mariposas monarcas que típicamente vuelan de nuestra región al norte y emprenden el largo vuelo de regreso a México donde pasan el invierno en un clima más cálido. Se cree que llevan consigo las almas de los difuntos que vuelven a visitar a sus familias. Es fácil ver por qué estas mensajeras aladas se consideran sagradas
posts.cp: Día de los Muertos has its roots in an Aztec ritual known as Miccaihuitl, honoring those who have passed

posts.c: For our 11th Month of Giving, we are thrilled to highlight the Green Mountain Club (GMC)! The Green Mountain Club is a nonprofit dedicated to getting YOU outside on Vermont’s hiking trails. They were founded more than 100 years ago to build the 272-mile Long Trail, which runs the length of Vermont from Massachusetts to Canada, and maintain the trail system to this day. Through sustainable trail work, strategic land conservation, free and low cost hiker education workshops and resources, and a robust community of volunteers and hikers, the Green Mountain Club ensures our beloved hiking trails are well cared for and accessible for all Vermonters to explore! To learn more, follow @greenmountainclub 💚

Our #WPY62 guest for this week is Oscar Whitfield! Oscar was crowned Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year with his striking image of a dung beetle followed by flies! 🪲 This week, he’ll be sharing his love of the African wildlife that live near his home – starting with these oxpeckers sitting on a zebra! 🦓 “While on a game drive near my home, we found a herd of zebras grazing on some green grass that had just come in from recent rainfall. While observing them, I realised that each zebra had its own family of red billed ox peckers on its back. The birds weren’t feeding, and looked quite wet from the rain that had just come, so it seemed like they were just resting there. I really liked the moment, resulting in me capturing the oxpeckers perched on the zebra’s back for ‘Stripes and Feathers’." - Oscar Whitfield Oscar is a young photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and still travels home in his school holidays, during which he spends a lot of time in Zambezi National Park. posts.c: I wish they had the slightest idea that how much they mean to us. Just yesterday, one of our cats disappeared out of sight for a few minutes as I’d left her chilling in the backyard. These are indoor cats, so they have absolutely zero clue about life beyond the four walls of our home & the little garden they know so well. And in those few moments, I went through an entire range of emotions. From panic to worry, from imagining all sorts of terrible possibilities to the fear of not knowing where she had gone. Meanwhile, 🐈 walked back in, completely unbothered, after her antics. 🤦🏻‍♀️ Also, as a cat owner, if there’s one thing I could recommend, it would be investing in a self-cleaning litter box. It has genuinely changed our lives, especially in a multi-cat household. Ours is a pretty old model, so it’s too big compared to the much smarter ones available these days. 🤌🏼 - - - #livingroom #bedroom #bluebedroom #cosybedroom #bedroomideas

posts.c: Have you seen a whale shark before? Alex Lindbloom’s (@alexlindbloomphoto) photo shows a whale shark investigating the catch of a 'bagan', or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua. He used the lights of the began to illuminate the sharks for his drone’s camera. Local fishing communities are using the predictable occurrence of whale sharks at bagans to attract tourists. Although contact with bagans can cause some minor injuries to whale sharks, this isn’t a major cause of mortality. Instead, the main reasons for the sharp decline in whale sharks in the Indo-Pacific region over the past 75 years are ship strikes, entanglements with fishing gear and illegal fishing. 📸 ‘Night-Time Catch’ is the winner of #WPY62's Oceans: The Bigger Picture category. Book your tickets for #WPY62 now via the link in our bio! #WPY #WildlifePhotographerOfTheYear #WildlifePhotography #NaturePhotography #NaturalHistoryMuseum #WhaleShark

posts.c: In celebration of Native American Heritage Month, we’re honored to share the powerful words and artistry of Joy Harjo, a citizen of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation and the first Native American to serve as United States Poet Laureate. Last year, we had the privilege of welcoming @joyharjoforreal to Longwood for a two-week residency as the inaugural recipient of our André Harvey Creative Fellowship. Rooted in Muscogee traditions and a lifetime of fearless creativity, she brought a powerful new voice to our landscapes and gifted us with a deeply moving presentation that includes reflections and readings from her award-winning body of work. We’re grateful for the wisdom, artistry, and perspective Harjo brought to Longwood, and delighted to share this special experience with you. 📽️ Watch the full presentation at the 🔗 in our bio. 📸 Carlos Alejandro

posts.c: The beauty of our world up-close 💚 "On a cool early morning at Pulborough Brooks RSPB, West Sussex, I came across this beautiful dragonfly resting on a blade of long grass, its body covered in delicate dew drops. The cold conditions meant the dragonfly remained still, giving me enough time to carefully capture a series of images for focus stacking. The tiny droplets created a wonderful pattern across its body, revealing the intricate beauty of this moment in nature. Sometimes, patience and the right conditions are all you need to turn an ordinary morning into something special." - Kutub Uddin (@kutub_uddin_macro_man) A big thank you to this week's #WPY62 guest, Kutub Uddin, winner of #WPY62's Portfolio Award, for showing us more of his incredible photography. Kutub is a macro photographer passionate about revealing the hidden beauty of the natural world. posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

A big yawn mid-stretch makes for a deceptive image. Most of us are aware that wolves do not impersonate grannies to trick children or huff and puff houses to the ground. Still, the archetype of the “big bad wolf” persists in folklore and fiction. Fairy tales like Little Red Riding Hood seem harmless enough, but as biodiversity plummets across the world, suddenly the fictitious villain becomes a very real and very convenient scapegoat. When local wildlife begins to decline, predators are often unfairly blamed for the loss, despite the fact that habitat destruction and development play a much larger role. My hope in sharing the beauty of animals like wolves in my new book Reverence is to inspire empathy and encourage us to reevaluate how we coexist with our planet’s predators. Visit the link in my bio to get your copy.

posts.c: When Halloween is over, look for Dracula in a hibernaculum! A hibernaculum is a place like a cave, den, or burrow, where animals seek shelter for the winter. At least 10 of Yellowstone’s 13 species of bats are winter hibernators. In the greater Yellowstone area, there are few known hibernacula, though researchers have identified some within the park. More surprising is that researchers have documented bat activity in Northern Yellowstone throughout the winter, despite little insect activity, and freezing cold temperatures. #BatWeek

posts.c: Happy Hubble Halloween! This new image of the Cat's Head Nebula shows a star-forming region with an eerily feline resemblance. The distinctive “cat’s head” shape of the nebula was likely sculpted over time by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars in the Carina Nebula, within which this nebula resides. Dare to learn more at the link in our bio! Image description: Visible-light image of the Cat’s Head Nebula by the Hubble Space Telescope. A dark brown, opaque filament of dust is in the center, stretching from the bottom to almost the very top. It has a narrow, irregular shape that resembles a cat sitting with its back toward the viewer and a tail extending downward. The cat’s head is turned toward the right, revealing a red glowing eye. The top half of the background is bright blue. Creepy Crawlers 🕷️: A Nephila clavipes (golden orb‑web spider) captured at the center of its web aboard the International Space Station. Researchers found that in the absence of gravity, the direction of light can serve as an orientation guide for spiders during web building. Credit: NASA Ghoulish Glow🔬: A miniaturized fluorescence microscope imaged fixed and live cells aboard the space station, helping advance fluorescence microscopy technology and allowing researchers to better evaluate cellular processes in microgravity. posts.c: Creating my book Reverence required endless hours of slogging through over 2 million images in my digital archives. In my bleary-eyed scrolling haze, I suddenly came across images I hadn’t seen in years. The polar bear above visited my cabin in the middle of a blizzard in Svalbard, and you can see in the series how she first peeked in before pawing at the window. The third image, titled Face to Face, became one of my best known prints and is the only image of mine I have ever felt compelled to hang my home. If you’d like to hear the full story in person, please join me Saturday Nov 14th at the @iconicimagesgallery in London for a special Q&A and book signing. Tickets are available through the link in my bio.

posts.c: Halloween is a time for things that go bump in the night. National parks have plenty of those. Boo! Still with us? From mysterious noises in the woods to wildlife that would prefer you keep your distance, the great outdoors can be downright spooky after dark. But the scariest encounters often have less to do with ghosts and more to do with poor planning, questionable decisions, and the occasional tree root working in cahoots with gravity. Whether you’re hiking a shadowy trail, camping beneath a full moon, or simply enjoying the autumn scenery, a few simple precautions can help keep your adventure from becoming a horror story. Stay on marked trails, watch your step, give wildlife plenty of space, check the weather, and pack the essentials. And if something in the woods starts whispering your name? posts.c: This spooky season, we're bringing you a tale of Halloween botany! The story begins with a dedicated search for the extremely rare and globally-vulnerable St. Lawrence grapefern (Sceptridium rugulosum). After weeks of combing potential habitat, one of our botanists was rewarded by finding this plant in a unique location — at the foot of a grave in a sandy cemetery in the Champlain Valley! While the location of this find is seasonally apropos, this is an exciting discovery for a more important reason: since the 90s, this species has been on the decline in Vermont. This find represents the first new population in Vermont in around 30 years, and this cemetery is currently the only known site for this rare grapefern in New England! Cemeteries often contain interesting plants that thrive in the low-competition environments created by consistent mowing as well as easy-to-dig-in sandy substrates. The tale of my spookiest adventure… and the only place I won’t hike again! 🔮✨ Deep in the hills above Eden is a section of the Long Trail known as Devil’s Gulch. You’d think a town named after the Garden of Eden wouldn’t have a haunted forest, but this is Vermont. Every forest is haunted… 🍂 In 1781, over 70 Green Mountain Boys were granted land here as a reward for fighting in the Revolution. Even though this area is stunning, none of them settled here. The hilly, rocky terrain offered little value for farming, and it was too removed from Vermont’s bustling towns. Whoever named this had a good sense of humor. At some point in Eden’s slow development, settlers found this ravine in the woods between Belvidere and Laraway Mountains. It became known as Devil’s Gulch, a term that dates back to the 1200s and means “to swallow greedily”. 🌿 This ravine is a defile, or place where the earth sort of burped, tossed up boulders, and dropped them in a jumble. These mossy, larger than life boulders

posts.c: Here’s looking at you, kid 👀👀👀👀 This Brazilian Whiteknee Tarantula is native to tropical areas of Brazil. Tarantula hair is adapted to help them sense vibrations and other stimuli, and some hairs are even barbed and can be used as a defensive mechanism. Many of us know tarantulas for their eight legs and two body segments, but there are other features that are characteristic of arachnids. If you look at a tarantula’s mouthparts, for instance, you will see chelicerae (jaw-like parts tipped with fangs) and a pair of pedipalps, which help them taste and hold their food. #tarantula #sandiegozoo

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. posts.c: What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science

This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: I asked, you answered. These are the Vermont sayings that came up again and again when I asked my Facebook followers, “What’s a Vermont saying that you don’t hear anywhere else?” “Dooryard” won by a landslide, but that was never used in my family growing up here. My grandmother loved to say something “had the radish” right before she threw it in the trash. 10: Had the radish: Worn out, broken, done for 9: Grinder: A sub sandwich 8: Hard tellin’, not knowin’: I can’t say until I know more 7: Prit near: Pretty near, almost 6: Creemee: Soft-serve ice cream, ideally maple 5: Wicked: Very 4: Flatlander: Anyone not from Vermont 3: You can’t get there from here: The road you want doesn’t connect to the road you’re on. Turn left where the barn used to be. 2: Jeezum Crow: How Vermonters swear without actually swearing. 1: Dooryard: The yard right outside your door, where you park and the kids play. posts.c: Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. While El Niño occurs in the Pacific Ocean, with changes most visible along the equator, its effects can be felt all around the world. NASA satellites like PACE and Sentinel-6 are equipped to measure some of the key features of the phenomenon. Video description: Three data visualizations stacked vertically show sea surface height, sea surface temperature, and ocean color from January 2026 to September 2026. As it plays, text forms across the screen that reads “We’re experiencing a record El Niño” and transitions to “Swipe to compare the growing 2026 El Niño with a weak La Niña in 2025.” Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Here's something to warm your heart on a chilly fall day! These clips of a Map Turtle hatchling emerging and being released into the Missisquoi Bay were captured by our biologists as they carried out turtle nest excavation last week at Sandy Point in Swanton. Turtle nests are carefully excavated for two main reasons: the first is so that we can document the number of successful nests and hatchlings produced, and the second is to protect live young still in the ground from being eaten by predators. The threatened Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle is the target species in this work, and three sites are managed for their nesting, with Sandy Point being historically the most important; however, other turtle species use the same beach, including Painted Turtles, Common Snapping Turtles, and Map Turtles, like the one seen here.

posts.c: Do you play Go? Simple rules. Endless possibilities. Over 2,500 years old, Go is a game where two players place black and white stones on a grid, competing to surround territory. It’s easy to learn the basics, with enough depth to keep you coming back for a lifetime. Remember Deep Blue beating chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997? It took almost two decades longer for AlphaGo to defeat Go legend Lee Sedol in 2016. That’s how much depth those little black and white stones hold. Roderick used to be big into Go, and he’s donated his board to Mesmer so you can enjoy it, too. Bring a friend, settle in, and play a game. And if Go isn’t your game, we have a full complement of other games to enjoy whenever we’re open. Come play. #kava #burlingtonvt #boardgames #go #nonalcoholic

posts.c: The original orange and black 🧡🖤 The San Diego Zoo and Safari Park care for two of the six tiger subspecies, Malayan and Sumatran. Their darker coats help them blend into shadows, and longer fur on their faces may help protect them from dense vegetation. Malayan tigers, native to the forests of the Malay Peninsula, have a slightly lighter coat that complements their surroundings. #sandiegozoo #sdzsafaripark #tiger

posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

posts.c: Each Tuesday this season, we're sharing stories that highlight what Rock Point means to you! "The cliffs rising over the Thrust Fault beach at Rock Point is one of the most beautiful places in Vermont! The stark juxtaposition of the dun colored Dolostone over the dark grey Iberville shale combined with the white cedars clinging to the cliffs is so dramatic. The fact that the top layer of rock is older than the bottom layer adds to the mystery. I have been leading trips to see this geologic feature for 40 years and it never ceases to amaze me and the people I am with. I always see wildlife at Rock Point from squirrels, foxes and mink to peregrines to ravens. Rock Point is a living sanctuary for people, plants and wild animals. It is truly the green heart of Burlington. I am so grateful to everyone who works to protect Rock Point's wild nature for us and for future generations." -Alicia Daniel, Director of Vermont Master Naturalist Have a testimonial you'd like to share? posts.c: After 38 wonderful years, The Vermont Pub & Brewery is sadly closing our doors. Since 2020, we’ve struggled to get back to the level of business that is necessary to sustain our operation, and unfortunately we just don’t have the resources to hold out any longer for that day to come. Our last full day of service will be Saturday, November 14th, three days after our 38th anniversary on November 11th. We owe a debt of gratitude to our beloved staff, past and present, as well as a myriad of regular patrons, many of whom have been coming in since day one! We are honored to have been a part of your lives for so many years, and we will truly miss you all. Greg's legacy does not end with the closing of VPB, but he will live on in our hearts and in every sip of Vermont craft beer and beyond. Stay tuned for upcoming beer and food specials!
posts.cp: After 38 wonderful years, The Vermont Pub & Brewery is sadly closing our doors

posts.c: Mr Creemee is 1 year old. He’s just a little baby! We opened our ice cream parlor October 26th of 2025. The months since then have been lovely and challenging, perhaps in equal parts. I’d like to simply express my gratitude to everyone who has supported us since then. There’s so much that goes into this kind of work, and sometimes it feels like a Sisyphean nightmare, but then someone says something nice about the ice cream and it makes the horrors go away. Jk jk. In reality this is my dream job and I’m grateful every day I get to spend with such wonderful people on both sides of the counter. posts.c: When a fire broke out at our Drop-Off Center in Williston early Tuesday morning, our staff knew exactly what to do. They called the fire department, followed safety protocols, and kept everyone safe- all skills and confidence learned from staff trainings. Throughout the year, we occasionally close our facilities so our staff can receive training on emergency response, hazardous materials handling, and workplace safety. We know closures can be inconvenient, and we’re so grateful for your patience and understanding during those closures. This week was a reminder of why those trainings really matter. Thank you to our staff for their dedication and to our community for supporting the work it takes to keep our facilities safe.
posts.hd: Staff gather outside for emergency response training

posts.c: You don’t need a garden bed to grow potatoes, and the science behind it is pretty cool. A seed potato already contains the energy and nutrients needed to kickstart new growth. Once it sprouts, the roots pull water and nutrients from the soil, while the leaves capture sunlight and convert it into energy that fuels the development of new potatoes underground. The tricky part is creating the right environment for those tubers. We’re using @foxfarmsoilandfertilizer Ocean Forest soil to give each potato a consistent growing medium with nutrients to support early growth. Potatoes need consistent moisture, but soil that stays too wet can limit oxygen around the roots and encourage rot. Good drainage helps maintain that balance, which is why the container you choose can make a bigger difference than you might expect. That’s what makes this potato experiment so interesting. Different containers can change how quickly soil dries out, how much heat it holds, and how easily excess water escapes. B

posts.c: What can you do to support biodiversity in your forest? Thoughtful forest management plays an important role in supporting and promoting biodiversity. Even small actions make a difference. 🪵 Embrace Messiness: Leave dead and downed trees to provide essential shelter, food, and nesting sites for wildlife. 🌳 Grow Trees of Different Ages: A mix of tree ages creates diverse habitats and resilient forests. 🌿Encourage Plant Diversity: Create space for native species to grow and protect young trees from being browsed by deer. 🌲 Maintain Connected Habitat Areas: Allow plants, animals, and fungi to move freely between your forest and neighboring lands and habitats. Ready to learn more? Check out the @uvmextforestry's new Forest Biodiversity website for educational guides and stewardship resources. Developed in partnership with @audubonvermont, @vtcoverts, Vermont Biodiversity Alliance, @vtforestsparksrecreation, and @vwatreefarm. 🔗Link in bio! Illustration by Carmen McFadden @propheticnewt

posts.c: This planet is haunted! 👻 The ghosts of volcanic eruptions, asteroid strikes, and evaporated lakes here on Earth are visible in echoes seen from space. Explore some of the places on our planet still haunted by the past. A volcanic eruption about 4,000 years ago created the eerily named Deception Island. The horseshoe-shaped island is actually the exposed part of a volcano itself, while the harbor in its center is a phantom of that massive volcanic eruption. As the volcano’s magma chamber emptied, the sudden drop in pressure inside the volcano caused the top to collapse and form a caldera — now called Port Foster. Image description: Landsat 8 image of Deception Island. It is horseshoe shaped and mostly rocky brown. The thin arch of rock comes to a ridge that runs the length of the island, along its center, like a backbone. posts.c: Ever look at all the rain hitting your roof and wonder how much water you’re letting go to waste? A rainwater capture system puts that water to work. Every inch of rain falling on a 1,000-square-foot roof can produce around 600 gallons of water. Gutters collect the runoff and direct it into a system that can help keep your garden watered. The science is all about collecting and filtering water before it reaches storage. A leaf filter catches larger debris, while a first flush diverter sends the dirtiest initial runoff away from the tank. This matters because dust, bird droppings, and other contaminants can build up on your roof between rainfalls. Removing that initial runoff helps keep your stored water cleaner. This rainwater capture system stores up to 5,750 gallons across the property, with underground pipes directing collected water into a main 5,000-gallon tank. posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Producer: Paul Morris Special thanks to Candy Jar, ASMR, and Donut Dan Music Credit: "Pizz with Pizzazz" by Bertrand Allagnat [SACEM] via Illustration Musicale [SACEM], Universal Productio

posts.c: So @jacquesinthegarden stumbled across a mystery pomegranate tree growing near his house, and the fruit turned out to be the sweetest he’d ever tasted. The science comes down to genetics. Pomegranates grown from seed can have a unique combination of genes from their parent plants, so the fruit may taste completely different from what you’d expect. That’s why this mystery tree outperformed one he had intentionally grown for three years. If you find a pomegranate with incredible flavor, you’ll want to clone it rather than grow it from seed. Hardwood cuttings can develop roots and grow into genetically identical plants, preserving the traits that made the original fruit so good. Keeping those cuttings warm while providing indirect light can help encourage root development, especially during cooler weather. And here’s the fun part: birds like crows can spread seeds to new places, creating unexpected seedlings throughout a neighborhood. You might not know what you’re growing until it fruits
posts.hd: Mystery pomegranate tree grows the sweetest fruit

posts.c: In the 1990s, George van Vlaanderen and Kristan Doolan made a decision that changed their lives: they started a farm. posts.c: We created a fleet of no-cost, seriously spooky, DIY witches brooms, with cuttings from our own yard.⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ Start by cutting small bundles of ornamental grass and hang them upside down to dry (you can skip the drying part). Cut branches to size (we got ours from our birch tree) and on one end wrap and knot twine - making sure to leave a 6” tail. Then, center the branch in a grass bundle before wrapping the grass with twine to keep it in place. Use the tail to tie off. Trim the grass to your desired length. Last, use a hook or just tie string around the other end of the branch to hang. ⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ We love the look and it was the perfect project to get us started on a very spooky exterior 🧙‍♀️⠀⠀ •⠀⠀ #renovationhusbands #diy #diydecor #halloween #halloweendecor diyhalloween

posts.c: Brewing up new stars 🪄 @NASAWebb’s unique view of the stellar nursery known as NGC 7129 reveals numerous stars formerly hidden in this cosmic cauldron. Stars begin their life in cold, dense regions of dust and gas, hiding from view of most telescopes. Webb’s high degree of infrared sensitivity allows astronomers to peer through dust to study these baby stars. In this image, we can see stars in various stages of development. The most mature and massive (about 5-8x the mass of our Sun) is the region’s bright central star. In the cavity on the left, appearing in gold, is the largest demonstration of its impact. The outflows from an earlier stage in the star’s development carve into the dense molecular cloud of hydrogen, and combine with the star’s light, causing it to glow. The region on the right, represented in red, hides much younger objects than those on the left: protostars. posts.c: He’s changed your life with dogs, and now, he’d like to change your dog’s life. Tomorrow, Elias Weiss Friedman, a.k.a. @TheDogist, is launching a brand dedicated to pet wellness, @TheDogistCompany, starting with an antioxidant soft-chew supplement. “This was a type of product that didn’t exist,” Friedman tells Forbes Vetted’s managing editor (and resident pet expert) Emmy Favilla of the Vitality antioxidant supplement, noting that it aims to fill a gap in the market and take the place of a multivitamin. Formulated with Dr. Angela Rollins, a board-certified veterinary nutritionist and clinical professor at the University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine (@utcvm), Vitality intends to reduce inflammation and support overall wellness, especially for picky eaters who aren’t eager for fruits and veggies, like Friedman’s own dog, Elsa. 🐶 The chew enters a market filled with pet multivitamins, which aren’t always a necessary addition to a dog’s diet. Vitality will be available for p

Today marks the beginning of a new chapter for The Dogist! 🎉I’m proud to announce the founding of @thedogistcompany and its first product: Vitality – Your dog’s daily dose of antioxidants (available at link in bio). Also featured today on @forbesvetted ! Elsa’s a picky eater (like many dogs), and refused to eat any healthy fruits or vegetables, like blueberries. This inspired me to partner with Dr. Angela Rollins, a Board Certified Veterinary Nutritionist (a rare speciality), to develop a new product that was different from any other dog health supplement on the market. We found that antioxidants, which help reduce oxidative stress on cells throughout the body, were missing from most fortified dog foods and supplements. Vitality was conceived, and after more than a year of development, it’s finally here! You can preorder your tin of Vitality right now at thedogistcompany.com! If you pre-order, tag @thedogist and @thedogistcompany and I’ll repost on my story!!

posts.c: Checking in on my Peace Lily - one of my first plants! - Light analysis: in a white LED grow light context, you need to specify the strength (FC or µmol/s/m² is fine) and the duration - you can calculate the DLI by multiplying the strength and the duration (along with the appropriate conversions) - For this plant: 90 FC x 14 hours gives you a DLI of 0.8 mol/day, which is quite low but clearly still enough to produce some flowers. With a higher DLI, my plant would have probably produced more flowers but I'm happy with where this plant is and how it has grown for now - The spent leaves on a peace lily don't tend to fall off on their own like a pothos or philodendron so you should regularly cut them off once they're fully dead - staying on top of it will allow space for new leaves to grow (mine has become a bit crowded!) - #houseplantjournal #peacelily #spathyphyllum

This is Harriet. She was found as a stray with chemical burns on her back and tail. Tests also showed that she has heartworm and lungworm infections, which caused a chronic cough that eventually led to bronchitis. She needs antibiotics to treat her burns, supportive care for her respiratory infections, and multiple rounds of heartworm injections. We don’t know how she ended up in this condition, but we do know that together, we can give her the care she deserves. held.c: Last week was tough for us. We were about to go on our daily walk, Kiki was on the couch while I put her harness on, I quickly went upstairs, and when I came back down, she was laying on the floor acting strange. When she got up, she was panting, drooling, and lifting her paw. It was 4pm on a Sunday, which meant the vets were closed. We had to drive 25 minutes to an emergency vet, they gave her pain meds and told us to keep an eye on her. On Monday morning, she was visibly in pain - as you can see in the first few clips. So we took her to the vet again. They told us - she has no noticeable fractures so you can either wait it out with her pain meds, or do an xray to find out more. We wanted to know more. And thank goodness we did… as it turned out, Kiki had hip dysplasia. One that you can tell it has most likely been there since she was a puppy - some dogs get it genetically. The thing is, Kiki, as probably most beagles… is such a sturdy, strong dog. The vets said she’s so visibly muscl

Ok people, It is Election Day and I hope you all know what that means! Time to go VOTE!! If you are like me, you may be saddened by the current political state in our country. Party allegiance aside, so much of what is being talked about seems to be fueled by hatred, violence and struggle. While It can all feel overwhelming, I always try and remember that the actual people who live in this country are loving, kind, hard working and resilient. When I was greeted with the above spread I was reminded about how great the people are and how important It is to elect leaders who think and act like us. The vast majority of us still do things because It helps to lift up our people, not because It is going to make us a billion dollars. This Election Day I will vote for the hard working Americans who deserve a better and easier path forward, and I will vote against the greedy and power obsessed billionaires who think they can run this country. Rest easy, Captain. We have the helm. ✨ Here is Webb’s look at Westerlund 1, a super star cluster - one of the closest clusters of its kind. Super star clusters are young and contain more than 10,000 times the mass of the Sun packed into a small volume. Westerlund 1 is the most massive yet identified in our galaxy, with 50,000 to 100,000 times the mass of the Sun contained within a region less than six light-years across. Super star clusters are one of the most extreme environments in which stars and planets can form. Because our galaxy is past its peak of star formation, and because such stars live relatively short lives, only a few of these clusters still exist to give us clues to that past era. What if you could turn a chicken into part of the process of growing a giant pumpkin? When Gucci, one of my original hens, passed away, I buried her beneath an Atlantic Giant pumpkin. Here’s the cool part: as bacteria and fungi break down organic matter, they recycle nutrients back into the soil. Plants can’t use all those nutrients immediately, though. Decomposition transforms them into forms roots can absorb, making decomposers an incredibly important part of a healthy garden. But growing a giant pumpkin takes more than nutrient-rich soil. I buried the vines so more nodes could develop roots, giving the plant additional access to water and nutrients. I removed competing flowers and fruits to focus the plant’s resources on one pumpkin, then added sand and plywood underneath to support its growing weight. Even with all those tricks, powdery mildew showed up and eventually slowed its growth. That’s what makes giant vegetables so fascinating: genetics, photosynthesis, growing conditions,

held.c: In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax. Rescued by PETA in 2010 at a year old, he was my shadow for the next 16+ years, sharing adventures and cuddles. His big brown eyes could stare into my soul and his big ears heard everything. He had quite the personality and loved to “talk,” and I quickly learned to understand his squeaks and groans. Jax was an excellent travel companion, happy to just be wherever I was. He was a master sunbather, always searching for the coziest spot in the house to catch some rays. In his younger years he loved to hike (and later enjoyed riding along in a backpack), and he was always ready to chase tennis balls or play tug-o’ -war until we were both exhausted. Then, he’d cuddle up next to me under a blanket, burrow his nose in, and snore and dream. At the end, with his face and muzzle nearly white, he was declining quickly and ready to go, and I was grateful to be able to give him a peaceful goodbye. Life isn’t the same without him,
held.cp: In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax

held.c: 10 years ago today, we received a mention from a man named Brant. What followed was an interaction that has quite literally changed my life. Brant received a lot of criticism for his words that day, but 2016 was a different, more graceful internet, and he rolled with the punches. He wore the “they’re good dogs Brent” merch we sent him, his Simpson’s themed wedding cake featured Santa’s Little Helper holding a sign featuring the phrase, and best of all, 2 years later, Brant got a dog. Completing potentially the most wholesome, full circle meme to ever exist. We haven’t heard from him in a few years, but Brant, wherever you are, give Charlie a hug from us ❤️
